items.full_text: Section 2. The Recruitment Crisis. The CDS told Parliament the CAF can only train 6,400 recruits per year through basic training. Months of underemployment after enrolment drives attrition. Her own words: there's no point in recruiting if you're not retaining people. Then the retention program was defunded. The Auditor General found the CAF failed to meet recruitment and training targets between April 2022 and March 2025. The mobilization directive targets 400,000 total force — but DND's own internal documents say supply chains and personnel systems are already at capacity.

items.full_text: Section 3. The Digital Battle Space. The Canadian Armed Forces has acknowledged that the information domain is a battle space. When the CDS restricts or disables public comment channels on official communications, that constitutes a surrender of ground in the digital battle space. The military's own doctrine recognizes information operations as a pillar of modern warfare. Ceding that ground to adversaries is a command failure.

items.page_title: CDS Accountability — Chief of the Defence Staff Record
items.full_text: Section 4. Foreign Military Access. Exercise PRECISE RESPONSE, June 2025, CFB Suffield: over 400 participants from 12 NATO nations conducted live-agent chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear training on Canadian soil. Canada is expanding Arctic training at Resolute Bay to near-permanent 10-month-per-year military presence, offering allied personnel Arctic training slots. 2,000 plus CAF members are on constant rotation in Latvia. Defence spending accelerated to 2 percent NATO target by 2027. The CDS frames this as requiring both international and domestic readiness simultaneously — while the domestic force hollows out.

items.page_title: CDS Accountability — Chief of the Defence Staff Record
items.full_text: Section 5. The Doublespeak Record. The CDS's own public statements contain documented contradictions. She says there's no point in recruiting if you're not retaining people — then the retention program is defunded. She says Canada has five years to prepare — then signs a mobilization directive that her own department says is impossible with current capacity. She establishes Cyber Command to contest the digital battle space — then restricts public engagement on official channels. Every statement is contradicted by the subsequent action. This is not incompetence. Incompetence is random. This is a pattern.

items.page_title: CDS Accountability — Chief of the Defence Staff Record

Section 46 — treason. Section 52 — sabotage. Section 122 — breach of trust. NDA section 73 — cowardice. NDA section 77 — cruelty of an officer. NDA section 84 — harbouring an enemy. These provisions exist. They have never been used against a Chief of the Defence Staff.

items.full_text: Lest We Forget. How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans. They were promised a country worthy of their sacrifice. They were given a backlog, a budget cut, and a brochure for medical assistance in dying.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 1. Veterans Affairs By the Numbers. A department failing the people it exists to serve. Over 11,000 veterans wait in the disability claims backlog while the department inexplicably lapses hundreds of millions in unspent funding.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 2. The Medical Assistance in Dying Question. Veterans who called seeking assistance for injuries sustained in service were systematically offered state-sponsored euthanasia. No veteran should ever be offered death when they are asking for help to live.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 3. The Funding Gap. Between 2018 and 2023, the government lapsed over 3 billion dollars in approved veterans funding. Money was budgeted, but Veterans Affairs simply failed to spend it on the people it was meant for.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 4. Phoenix Pay and Veterans. Broken Twice. The 2.2 billion dollar Phoenix Pay failure devastated veterans transitioning to federal employment, leaving many without paychecks while simultaneously navigating the disability backlog.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 5. The Office Closures. In 2014, the Harper government closed 9 Veterans Affairs district offices across Canada. Veterans in rural and remote communities lost face-to-face access to caseworkers. Some had to travel hundreds of kilometres for appointments. Many simply stopped seeking help.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 6. Operational Stress Injuries. The invisible wounds. Post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, and moral injury affect tens of thousands of Canadian veterans. Wait times for mental health services at Veterans Affairs routinely exceed 6 months. The veteran suicide rate remains significantly higher than the general population.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 7. The Record of Broken Promises. Decade after decade, Canadian governments have promised veterans better care, faster processing, more support. And decade after decade, those promises have been broken. The Veterans Charter was supposed to fix everything. It didn't. The New Veterans Charter was supposed to modernize everything. It created new problems.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Section 8. Source Attribution. Every number, every claim, every fact on this page comes from the public record: Auditor General reports, Parliamentary Budget Officer analyses, Veterans Affairs annual reports, House of Commons committee testimony, and court documents. Nothing is alleged without attribution.

items.page_title: Lest We Forget — How Canada Betrayed Its Veterans
items.full_text: Lest We Forget. Those words are carved into cenotaphs across this country. But we have forgotten. We forgot when we closed their offices. We forgot when we let billions lapse unspent. We forgot when we offered them death instead of help. Every veteran who served this country was promised that Canada would take care of them. Canada broke that promise.

items.full_text: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data. Higher suicide rates. Months-long waits for disability benefits. And when they ask for a wheelchair ramp, they're offered death. Every number below comes from the Government of Canada's own reports.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: Veteran suicide. Male veterans die by suicide at 1.4 times the civilian rate. Female veterans at 1.9 times. This elevated risk has persisted for forty-two years. The government has known.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: The disability benefits backlog. Only forty-seven percent of applications now meet the sixteen-week standard. The backlog doubled from five thousand six hundred to over eleven thousand in a single year.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: Mental health claim denials. Of fifteen thousand veterans who applied for mental health disability benefits, twenty-four percent were denied. Nearly one in four told their suffering does not qualify.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.summary: MAID — offered death instead of help.
items.full_text: MAID — offered death instead of help. A Paralympian veteran asked for a wheelchair ramp. The government's response: we can help you die. At least four to five confirmed cases of veterans being offered MAID by a Veterans Affairs employee.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: The math. A MAID procedure costs twenty-five hundred dollars. A wheelchair ramp costs three to eight thousand. Annual disability benefits cost fifteen to forty thousand per veteran. It is cheaper to kill a veteran than to provide a ramp for two years.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: My case. A veteran reported foreign interference targeting the mental health infrastructure that serves soldiers. The response was not investigation. It was prosecution. The message: stay silent or be destroyed.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: Veteran homelessness. Three to five thousand Canadian veterans are homeless on any given night. Veterans are overrepresented in shelter populations by two to four times their proportion of the general population.

items.page_title: How Canada Treats Its Veterans — The Data
items.full_text: The veteran-to-MAID pipeline. Inadequate transition, denied claims, impossible wait times, and then an offer of death. The government's own data documents every link in this chain. This is not random failure. It is a connected pipeline.

Canada's Broken Whistleblower Protection. Hundreds of complaints filed. Virtually zero successful prosecutions for reprisal. Maximum compensation: $10,000. Canada doesn't protect the brave. It destroys them.

Section 1. The Protection That Doesn't Exist. The Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act was supposed to shield whistleblowers. Over seventeen years, the numbers tell the story of a law that exists on paper and nowhere else.

Section 2. The Mark Norman Case. The Vice-Admiral was destroyed for ensuring a critical naval supply contract wasn't killed by political interference. The charges collapsed, but the message was unmistakable: challenge political interference and we will destroy you.

Section 3. Richard Colvin. When a Canadian diplomat reported that Afghan detainees were being transferred to face torture, his government attacked his character and threatened him with prosecution under the Security of Information Act.

Section 4. Cameron Ortis. The Director General of RCMP Intelligence operated as a mole for years. If the RCMP cannot police its own intelligence directorate, it cannot be trusted to investigate reprisal complaints from whistleblowers.

Section 5. Other notable cases — the parade of destruction. Sylvie Therrien exposed fraud in EI processing and was fired. Sean Bruyea's medical records were shared across 100 bureaucrats in retaliation. Edgar Schmidt challenged the government's legal opinion process and was suspended. The pattern is always the same: speak the truth, lose your career.

Section 6. The Public Sector Integrity Commissioner — the watchdog that doesn't bite. In 17 years, PSIC has found wrongdoing in fewer than 10 cases. Hundreds of disclosures have been dismissed. The Commissioner lacks subpoena power, cannot protect witnesses, and reports to the same government whose misconduct is being reported.

Section 7. International comparison — dead last among allies. The United States has the False Claims Act with qui tam provisions. The UK has the Public Interest Disclosure Act. Australia has a National Anti-Corruption Commission. Canada has none of these. Among Five Eyes nations, Canada ranks last in whistleblower protection.

Section 8. What real protection looks like. A Canadian False Claims Act with financial rewards for whistleblowers who expose fraud. An independent protection agency outside political control. Reverse burden of proof — employers must prove reprisal was not a factor. Criminal penalties for retaliation. These are not radical proposals. They exist in every allied nation except Canada.

The Criminal Code irony. Canada's Criminal Code contains no specific offence for retaliating against a whistleblower. A government employee who exposes billions in fraud has no legal shield. The person who fires them faces no criminal consequence. The law protects the institution, not the individual who tries to fix it.
